name: The water table that does no work
symptom: A horizontal band at the base of the wall that is a flat 1x board or a foam bump in the same plane as the cladding, with no wash on its top, no drip on its underside, and no wall-thickness change behind it. Water runs down the cladding, across the board, and back onto the wall below. In the worst version the 'water table' is a strip of a different siding colour.

cause.explanation: The water table is scheduled as trim, so it is bought as a 1x8 or a 5/4x8 in the same PVC or fibre-cement family as the corner boards. Stock trim is flat with a square edge; a bevelled cap with a drip kerf is a milled item that must be ordered, and the crew must then rip a bevel and cut a kerf on every board. In a veneer or a rainscreen there is also nothing behind it — the wall is one thickness top to bottom — so there is genuinely no step to weather and the board becomes an appliqué by default.
cause.cost_saved: A milled water table with a bevelled cap, drip kerf and metal flashing runs $18-$34 per lineal foot against $7-$12 for a flat board. On 160 lf that is $1,800-$3,500.

rule_violated.statement: A moulded or bevelled water table runs 24 to 36 in above finished grade, projects about 2 in, and returns fully round every elevation of the volume including the rear.

rule_violated.ref: brick-course / water_table.projection = part * 0.75 = 2 1/16 in; water_table.height = module * 2.5 = 27 1/2 in (ten courses)
rule_violated.statement: About two inches of projection — one course set out — landing on a whole course.

rule_violated.ref: facade-classical / elevation.water_table: height_parts 0.75 (6 3/4 in), projection_parts 0.35 (3 1/8 in)
rule_violated.statement: Either way it is a real change of wall thickness, not a stuck-on trim, and that is why it is allowed to be the strongest horizontal below the cornice.

correct_practice: The water table is the top of the base and the point at which the wall steps IN. In masonry it is a moulded, chamfered or bevelled course set out about 2 in with the wall above stepping back by half a brick (4.5 in at a floor, 2 in at the water table); in frame it is a board 6 3/4 to 9 in deep with a weathered cap sloping 15-30 degrees, projecting 2 to 3 1/8 in past the cladding above, with a drip kerf or a chamfered underside and a metal cap flashing lapping under the cladding. It sits 24-36 in above finished grade — ten brick courses where the wall is brick — and it returns fully round every elevation including the rear. It must project more than the belt course above it and less than the cornice: water table 3 1/8 in, belt 2 1/4 in, cornice 7 3/4 in on the default bay is the whole discipline of the front in three numbers.

fixes.right: Mill the cap: a 5/4 board with the top ripped to a 20 degree wash, a 3/8 in drip kerf 1/2 in back from the front edge on the underside, set out on furring so its face stands 2-3 in proud of the cladding above, with a stainless or copper cap flashing behind. Return it round every elevation.
fixes.cheap: Fur it out. Nail the existing flat stock trim over a continuous 2x2 ripped to a wash — about $1.10 per lineal foot in material — and chamfer the bottom front edge with two passes of a block plane or a router. This produces 2 1/2 in of projection, a shed and a drip for under $3/lf and no change to the schedule. The projection matters far more than the moulding profile: a plain square board standing 2 1/2 in proud outperforms an elaborate ovolo standing 3/4 in proud at every viewing distance.
fixes.dishonest: A darker paint colour on the flat band to make it read as a base. This is the flat-elevation habit at its purest: it survives in a photograph taken in overcast light and disappears the moment the sun comes out and the eye starts looking for the shadow it expects. It also puts a hard colour line where the wall has no joint, which is the colour version of the flush material change.

detection: Look for the shadow under the band, and measure it. In an image with any directional light, a working water table casts a continuous shadow 1 1/2 to 3 in deep on the wall below it; a flat trim board casts a hairline or none. Measure the band's projection against a known dimension in the same photograph — a clapboard butt is 3/4 in, a brick is 2 1/4 in high. Projection under 1 in is the fault. Second test: the top edge. If the top of the band is horizontal and meets the cladding above in a caulk joint, it has no wash and water is being held on it — look for the dirt line and the paint failure that always follow, usually visible as a grey streak in a photograph of a five-year-old house. Third: follow it round the corner. It should return; a water table that stops at the front corner is two faults at once.

exceptions.why: No applied trim of any kind on the exterior; the base is expressed by a batter in the wall itself.
exceptions.bounds: There must be an actual batter of 2-6 in over the lowest 24-36 in. A vertical stucco wall with no water table and no batter has simply omitted the base.

bounds_test.note: A measurable widening of 2-6 in over the lowest 24-36 in. A vertical stucco wall with no water table and no batter has simply omitted the base.

applies_when.note: The wall must do the work the trim is not doing.

exceptions.why: Trim suppression is the style's argument; a water table would interrupt the continuous skin. The base is expressed by a stone ground storey or by a flared shingle course.
exceptions.bounds: A flare — doubled or tripled shingle butts standing 1-2 in proud over 2-3 courses — is doing the work and must be present. Nothing at all is not the exception.

bounds_test.note: Doubled or tripled butts standing 1-2 in proud over 2-3 courses. Nothing at all is not the exception.

applies_when.note: Holds only where primary_cladding is shingle carried to the base.

exceptions.why: Greek Revival flattens mouldings on purpose; its water table is often a plain unmoulded board with a simple bevel and no ovolo.
exceptions.bounds: Flat profile, full projection. The board still stands 2-3 in proud and still has a wash. Greek Revival simplifies the section; it does not delete the depth.

bounds_test.note: Flat profile, full projection. Greek Revival simplifies the section and does not delete the depth; the numeric test is entirely unchanged, only the moulding vocabulary drops out.

applies_when.note: Plain bevelled board rather than an ovolo — a profile change, not a dimension change.

exceptions.why: The base is expressed by a painted skirting band — ochre or blue, 800-1000 mm high — carried over a continuously rendered wall, with no projection at all.
exceptions.bounds: This is a colour base on a genuinely massive lime-rendered wall (500-700 mm), where the wall's mass is already evident at every reveal. It is not a licence to paint a stripe on a stud wall.

bounds_test.note: 500 mm. A painted skirting band of 800-1000 mm is a colour base on a genuinely massive lime-rendered wall whose mass is already evident at every reveal. It is not a licence to paint a stripe on a stud wall.

confused_with.difference: There the water table is absent altogether; here it is present and inert. The detection is different: absence is easier to see than inadequacy, which is why this fault survives review more often.
Same family of horizontal, different position and different rule. The belt is placed by the section; the water table is placed by the grade.

sources: NPS Preservation Brief 39: Holding the Line: Controlling Unwanted Moisture

test.note: Two inches — one brick course set out (brick-course gives part * 0.75 = 2 1/16 in; facade-classical gives 0.35 parts = 3 1/8 in). Measure against a known dimension in the same photograph: a clapboard butt is 3/4 in, a brick 2 1/4 in high. Under 1 in it is not a transition, it is a caulk joint. Projection matters far more than profile: a plain square board at 2 1/2 in proud outperforms an elaborate ovolo at 3/4 in at every viewing distance.

secondary_tests.note: The hierarchy of horizontals: water table 3 1/8 in, belt 2 1/4 in, cornice 7 3/4 in on the default bay. The water table must out-project the belt above it. Where a house has both, this is a free check that needs no absolute scale.
Ten brick courses where the wall is brick. This is the datum the whole elevation is measured up from.

A wash of 15-30 degrees plus a drip kerf. A horizontal top meeting the cladding above in a caulk joint holds water, and the evidence is visible in a photograph of a five-year-old house as a grey dirt streak and a line of paint failure.

severity_trajectory: Minor to serious over 5-10 years. A water table with no wash and no drip holds water at the joint with the cladding above and returns it to the wall below; the sequence is dirt streaking, then paint failure along the top edge, then rot or spalling in the base course. The visual fault and the fabric fault have the same cause, which is why the fix is one detail rather than two.

severity_by_style.why: No applied trim of any kind; the base is a batter in the wall itself.
The kit forbids 'none' outright: a brick wall that starts at grade has no plinth and the house appears dropped rather than built.

inverted_by.statement: A projecting moulded water table is the fault here. The base is expressed by a batter of 2-6 in over the lowest 24-36 in and by nothing else; any applied horizontal is foreign to the style.
A water table interrupts the continuous skin and is the fault. The base is expressed by a flared shingle course standing 1-2 in proud, or by a stone ground storey, and by no trim.
